# Overview



Nicheformer is a foundation model designed for single-cell and spatial omics analysis, leveraging transformer architecture to learn comprehensive representations from gene expression data across multiple technologies and tissues. The project provides pretrained models, training pipelines, and tools for downstream analysis tasks including classification, regression, and embedding extraction. By training on large-scale multi-technology datasets like the SpatialCorpus-110M, Nicheformer learns transferable representations that capture fundamental biological patterns in cellular microenvironments across diverse experimental conditions.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L65), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L45)

## Architecture and Design

Nicheformer implements a transformer-based architecture optimized for gene expression data analysis, following the masked language modeling paradigm similar to BERT but adapted for spatial transcriptomics. The core model architecture consists of 12 transformer layers with 16 attention heads, a 512-dimensional model representation, and 1024-dimensional feedforward layers. The model processes tokenized gene expression sequences with a context length of 1500 tokens, incorporating auxiliary tokens to encode metadata such as species, assay type, and tissue modality, enabling it to learn technology-agnostic representations.

The data processing pipeline transforms raw gene expression matrices into tokenized sequences using technology-specific mean vectors. Spatial data incorporates neighborhood information through niche composition features (X_niche_0 through X_niche_4), representing the top 5 most frequent cell types in each cell's microenvironment. This design allows the model to learn both intrinsic gene expression patterns and spatial context simultaneously. The system supports both dissociated single-cell data and spatial transcriptomics technologies including CosMX, MERFISH, Xenium, and ISS.

Sources: [src/nicheformer/models/_nicheformer.py](src/nicheformer/models/_nicheformer.py#L1-L100), [src/nicheformer/data/datamodules.py](src/nicheformer/data/datamodules.py#L14-L54), [src/nicheformer/config_files/_config_train.py](src/nicheformer/config_files/_config_train.py#L1-L26)

## Core Components

The Nicheformer framework is organized into four main functional areas: data processing and tokenization, model training and pretraining, fine-tuning for downstream tasks, and embedding extraction for analysis. The data module provides utilities for filtering, normalization, and tokenization of gene expression data, with specialized support for niche composition analysis in spatial datasets. The training module implements distributed training using PyTorch Lightning, supporting multi-GPU setups and experiment tracking through Weights & Biases.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[Raw Gene Expression Data] --> B[Data Processing & Tokenization]
    B --> C[NicheformerDataset]
    C --> D[Merlin DataLoaders]
    D --> E["Pretraining<br/>Masked Token Prediction"]
    D --> F["Fine-tuning<br/>Classification/Regression"]
    D --> G[Embedding Extraction]
    E --> H[Pretrained Model]
    F --> I[Specialized Task Models]
    G --> J[Cell Embeddings]
    H --> F
    H --> G
    J --> K[Downstream Analysis]
    I --> K
```

The model architecture includes a standard Transformer encoder with learnable positional embeddings, supporting configuration for auxiliary tokens including specie, assay, and modality embeddings. During pretraining, the model uses masked token prediction with a 15% masking probability, following a distribution where 80% of masked tokens are replaced with a mask token, 10% with random tokens, and 10% kept unchanged. This strategy enables the model to learn robust representations while preventing trivial solutions.

Sources: [src/nicheformer/models/_nicheformer.py](src/nicheformer/models/_nicheformer.py#L62-L100), [src/nicheformer/models/_utils.py](src/nicheformer/models/_utils.py#L9-L63), [src/nicheformer/_train.py](src/nicheformer/_train.py#L8-L81)

## Project Structure

The repository follows a modular structure separating core functionality from configuration and experiments. The source code is organized in the `src/nicheformer/` directory, with main entry points for training (`train.py`), fine-tuning (`fine_tune.py`), and embedding extraction (`get_embeddings.py`). Configuration files are centralized in `config_files/`, providing easy customization for different workflows. The `data/` directory contains pretrained model weights and loading scripts for the SpatialCorpus-110M dataset.

```
nicheformer/
├── src/nicheformer/          # Core source code
│   ├── models/               # Model architectures
│   │   ├── _nicheformer.py  # Main transformer model
│   │   ├── _fine_tune_model.py
│   │   └── _utils.py        # Utility functions
│   ├── data/                 # Data processing modules
│   │   ├── dataset.py       # Dataset implementation
│   │   ├── datamodules.py   # Merlin data loaders
│   │   └── tools/           # Data processing utilities
│   ├── experiments/         # Experiment scripts
│   └── config_files/        # Configuration modules
├── data/                     # Data and model weights
│   ├── model_means/         # Technology mean vectors
│   └── spatialcorpus-110M/  # Dataset loading scripts
├── notebooks/                # Example notebooks
│   ├── experiments/          # Training and fine-tuning
│   └── tokenization/         # Data tokenization examples
└── docs/                     # Documentation
```

Configuration-driven design allows researchers to easily adapt the system to their specific use cases. Key configuration parameters include model architecture dimensions (dim_model, nheads, nlayers), training hyperparameters (learning rate, warmup steps, batch size), and data specifications (context_length, n_tokens, masking_p). The system supports multiple downstream tasks including classification tasks (e.g., cell type annotation), regression tasks (e.g., density prediction), and embedding extraction for unsupervised analysis.

Sources: [src/nicheformer/__init__.py](src/nicheformer/__init__.py#L1-L8), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L1-L5), [notebooks/README.md](notebooks/README.md#L1-L5)

## Supported Technologies and Applications

Nicheformer supports a wide range of single-cell and spatial transcriptomics technologies, making it applicable to diverse research scenarios. For spatial technologies, the system includes tokenization notebooks for CosMX (human liver and lung), MERFISH (mouse brain), and Xenium (human colon and lung). For dissociated single-cell data, it supports standard scRNA-seq datasets and in situ sequencing (ISS) technologies. This broad compatibility enables cross-technology transfer learning and generalization across tissue types and experimental platforms.

> [!TIP]
> The model's strength lies in its ability to learn unified representations from heterogeneous data sources, making it particularly valuable for cross-technology analysis and transfer learning scenarios where limited training data is available for specific platforms or tissues.

Pretrained model weights are available for download from Mendeley Data, providing researchers with models trained on the complete SpatialCorpus-110M dataset containing 110 million cells across multiple technologies and tissues. These pretrained weights can be used for direct embedding extraction or as initialization points for fine-tuning on specific downstream tasks. The fine-tuning pipeline supports flexible layer extraction strategies, allowing researchers to choose which layers to use for specific applications or reinitialize layers for better adaptation to new tasks.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L38-L44), [data/spatialcorpus-110M/README.md](data/spatialcorpus-110M/README.md#L1-L9), [notebooks/experiments/get_embeddings.ipynb](notebooks/experiments/get_embeddings.ipynb#L1-L80)

## Key Features and Capabilities

Nicheformer provides several advanced features that distinguish it from other single-cell analysis frameworks. Distributed training support enables efficient training on large datasets across multiple GPUs, leveraging PyTorch Lightning for simplified multi-device orchestration. The data loading pipeline uses Merlin dataloaders optimized for large-scale Parquet datasets, supporting efficient data streaming and memory management for datasets with millions of cells. Experiment tracking integration with Weights & Biases facilitates reproducible research and systematic hyperparameter optimization.

The tokenization strategy preserves biological information while enabling efficient model training. Gene expression values are normalized and tokenized using technology-specific mean vectors, accounting for systematic differences between platforms. For spatial data, the system incorporates niche composition features by counting the top 5 most frequent cell types in each cell's neighborhood, providing the model with explicit spatial context information. This design enables the model to learn representations that capture both gene expression patterns and spatial relationships simultaneously.

Configuration flexibility allows researchers to adapt the system to their specific needs. The three main workflows—training, fine-tuning, and embedding extraction—are each configured through dedicated configuration modules. Key configuration options include architectural dimensions, training hyperparameters, data specifications, and task-specific settings. This modular design supports rapid experimentation and facilitates systematic comparison of different modeling approaches.

Sources: [src/nicheformer/data/datamodules.py](src/nicheformer/data/datamodules.py#L56-L91), [src/nicheformer/config_files/_config_train.py](src/nicheformer/config_files/_config_train.py#L1-L26), [src/nicheformer/fine_tune.py](src/nicheformer/fine_tune.py#L1-L17)

## Getting Started

To begin using Nicheformer, you'll need to install the package in a Python 3.9+ environment. The recommended approach is to create a dedicated conda environment and install from source using the development version. After installation, you can access pretrained model weights and technology mean vectors from Mendeley Data, placing them in the `data/` subdirectory. The project provides example notebooks demonstrating common workflows including data tokenization for various technologies, embedding extraction from pretrained models, and fine-tuning for downstream classification or regression tasks.

The three primary use cases for Nicheformer correspond to the three main entry points: `train.py` for pretraining new models from scratch, `fine_tune.py` for adapting pretrained models to specific downstream tasks, and `get_embeddings.py` for extracting cell-level representations from existing models. Each workflow has its own configuration file in `config_files/`, allowing you to customize parameters without modifying source code. The notebooks directory provides concrete examples for each of these workflows, with technology-specific tokenization examples for the supported platforms.

For beginners, we recommend starting with the embedding extraction workflow to become familiar with the data format and model outputs before attempting training or fine-tuning. The [Quick Start](2-quick-start) guide provides step-by-step instructions for this workflow, while subsequent sections cover installation, data downloading, and advanced usage patterns. As you become more comfortable with the system, you can explore fine-tuning for specific research questions or even train custom models on your own datasets.


# Quick Start



Nicheformer is a foundation model for single-cell and spatial omics data that enables powerful analysis across multiple technologies and tissue types. This guide will help you get up and running quickly with pre-trained models, allowing you to extract cell embeddings and fine-tune the model for your specific downstream tasks. Nicheformer leverages a transformer architecture trained on large-scale spatial and dissociated transcriptomics data, making it particularly effective for niche composition analysis and transfer learning across different omics modalities.

## Project Overview

Nicheformer provides two primary workflows: extracting embeddings from pre-trained models for downstream analysis, and fine-tuning the model for specific supervised tasks. The framework is built on PyTorch Lightning and supports distributed training with Merlin DataModule for efficient data loading at scale.

![Nicheformer Architecture](https://github.com/theislab/nicheformer/blob/main/docs/notebooks/example.ipynb?raw=true)

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    A[Raw Omics Data<br/>AnnData format] --> B[Data Tokenization<br/>Technology-specific means]
    B --> C{Choose Workflow}
    C --> D[Extract Embeddings]
    C --> E[Fine-tune Model]
    D --> F[Pre-trained Nicheformer<br/>Backbone]
    E --> F
    F --> G[Cell Embeddings<br/>512-dimensional vectors]
    E --> H[Task-Specific Head<br/>Classification/Regression]
    G --> I[Downstream Analysis<br/>Clustering, Visualization]
    H --> J[Supervised Predictions<br/>Cell types, densities]
```

The project structure follows a modular design separating models, data processing, and experiment configurations:

![Project Structure](https://github.com/theislab/nicheformer/blob/main/src/nicheformer/__init__.py?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L1-L15), [__init__.py](src/nicheformer/__init__.py#L5-L8)

## Installation

Nicheformer requires Python 3.9 or newer. We strongly recommend creating a fresh conda environment to avoid dependency conflicts:

```bash
# Create a new environment
mamba create -n nicheformer_env python=3.9
mamba activate nicheformer_env

# Clone and install development version
git clone https://github.com/theislab/nicheformer.git
cd nicheformer
pip install -e .
```

The installation includes core dependencies for deep learning (PyTorch, PyTorch Lightning), data handling (AnnData, NumPy), distributed training (Merlin, Dask), and visualization (Squidpy). For GPU acceleration, consider installing CUDA dependencies with `pip install -e ".[cuda]"`.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L16-L33), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L52)

## Downloading Pre-trained Models

Pre-trained model weights and technology-specific mean files are available from Mendeley Data. Download these files into the `data/` subdirectory in the repository:

- **Pre-trained model**: `nicheformer.ckpt` - The foundation model pre-trained on the SpatialCorpus-110M dataset
- **Technology means**: Mean vectors for normalizing data from different platforms (CosMX, MERFISH, Xenium, ISS, dissociated scRNA-seq)
- **Example data**: Sample AnnData files demonstrating proper data formatting

```bash
# After downloading from Mendeley Data, organize as:
data/
├── nicheformer.ckpt
├── model_means/
│   ├── cosmx_mean_script.npy
│   ├── merfish_mean_script.npy
│   ├── xenium_mean_script.npy
│   └── dissociated_mean_script.npy
└── model.h5ad
```

These assets are essential for both embedding extraction and fine-tuning workflows. The technology mean files ensure proper normalization across different platforms using the tokenization pipeline.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L40-L44), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L1-L5)

## Quick Workflows

Nicheformer supports two main entry points depending on your analysis needs:

| Workflow | Purpose | Output | Complexity |
|----------|---------|--------|------------|
| **Extract Embeddings** | Get fixed representations for downstream analysis | Cell embeddings (512-dim vectors) in AnnData | Beginner |
| **Fine-tune Model** | Adapt model to specific supervised tasks | Task-specific predictions (classification/regression) | Intermediate |

### Getting Cell Embeddings

Extracting embeddings is the quickest way to leverage Nicheformer for exploratory analysis. This workflow uses the pre-trained model as a feature extractor without modifying its weights:

```python
import anndata as ad
from nicheformer.models import Nicheformer
from nicheformer.data import NicheformerDataset
import torch

# Load your data
adata = ad.read_h5ad('path/to/your/data.h5ad')
technology_mean = np.load('path/to/technology_mean.npy')

# Create dataset
dataset = NicheformerDataset(
    adata=adata,
    technology_mean=technology_mean,
    max_seq_len=1500,
    aux_tokens=30
)

# Load pre-trained model
model = Nicheformer.load_from_checkpoint('data/nicheformer.ckpt')
model.eval()

# Extract embeddings
dataloader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=32)
embeddings = []
for batch in dataloader:
    with torch.no_grad():
        output = model.get_embeddings(batch, layer=-1)
        embeddings.append(output.cpu().numpy())

# Store in AnnData
adata.obsm['nicheformer_embeddings'] = np.concatenate(embeddings, axis=0)
```

The resulting embeddings can be used for clustering, visualization (UMAP/t-SNE), or as input to downstream machine learning models. The `get_embeddings` method accepts a `layer` parameter to extract features from different transformer depths (-1 for the last layer).

Sources: [get_embeddings.ipynb](notebooks/experiments/get_embeddings.ipynb#L1-L80), [_embeddings.py](src/nicheformer/_embeddings.py#L8-L100), [Nicheformer.get_embeddings](src/nicheformer/models/_nicheformer.py#L272-L274)

### Fine-tuning for Downstream Tasks

For supervised tasks like cell type classification or niche density prediction, fine-tuning adapts the pre-trained backbone to your specific problem:

```python
from pytorch_lightning import Trainer
from nicheformer.models import Nicheformer, NicheformerFineTune

# Load pre-trained backbone
backbone = Nicheformer.load_from_checkpoint('data/nicheformer.ckpt')

# Create fine-tuning model
fine_tune_model = NicheformerFineTune(
    backbone=backbone,
    supervised_task='niche_regression',
    extract_layers=[11],  # Use last layer features
    function_layers='mean',
    lr=1e-4,
    warmup=10,
    max_epochs=100,
    dim_prediction=33,  # Output dimension for niche composition
    freeze=False  # Allow backbone adaptation
)

# Configure trainer
trainer = Trainer(
    max_epochs=100,
    accelerator='gpu',
    devices=1,
    precision='bf16-mixed'
)

# Train (assuming you have train/val splits)
trainer.fit(fine_tune_model, train_dataloader, val_dataloader)
```

Fine-tuning supports multiple task types through the `supervised_task` parameter:
- `niche_regression`: Predict continuous niche composition values
- `density_regression`: Predict cell density
- `niche_classification`: Classify cells into categories
- Custom configurations via `dim_prediction` and `n_classes`

Sources: [downstream_fine_tune.ipynb](notebooks/experiments/downstream_fine_tune.ipynb#L1-L120), [_fine_tune.py](src/nicheformer/_fine_tune.py#L8-L75), [NicheformerFineTune](src/nicheformer/models/_nicheformer_fine_tune.py#L15-L80)

## Data Preparation Requirements

Before using Nicheformer, your data must be properly formatted and tokenized. The framework expects AnnData objects with specific structure:

### Essential AnnData Structure

```
adata:
├── X: Gene expression matrix (cells × genes), sparse or dense
├── obs: Cell metadata
│   └── nicheformer_split: 'train', 'val', or 'test' partition
└── var: Gene metadata (must match gene set used during pre-training)
```

> [!TIP]
> Ensure your gene expression matrix uses the same gene ordering as the pre-trained model. The gene mapping is stored in `data/model.h5ad` and should be used to align your data before tokenization.

### Tokenization Process

Gene expression values are converted to integer tokens using technology-specific mean values:

```python
from nicheformer.data.dataset import tokenize_data

# Normalize and tokenize
tokens = tokenize_data(
    x=adata.X.toarray() if hasattr(adata.X, 'toarray') else adata.X,
    median_counts_per_gene=technology_mean,
    max_seq_len=1500  # Context window size
)
```

The tokenization process:
1. Applies size-factor normalization to scale counts to 10,000
2. Discretizes expression values into integer tokens
3. Truncates or pads sequences to `max_seq_len`
4. Reserves auxiliary tokens for special purposes (CLS, MASK, etc.)

Sources: [dataset.py](src/nicheformer/data/dataset.py#L12-L50), [tokenization example](notebooks/tokenization/xenium_human_lung.ipynb#L1-L80)

## Configuration System

Nicheformer uses YAML-style configuration dictionaries to manage experiment parameters. Key configuration files are located in `src/nicheformer/config_files/`:

### Embedding Configuration

```python
sweep_config = {
    'checkpoint_path': "data/nicheformer.ckpt",
    'fine_tuned_checkpoint_path': "data/nicheformer_ft.ckpt",
    'organ': "everything"  # Data partition to process
}
```

### Fine-tuning Configuration

```python
sweep_config = {
    'checkpoint_path': "data/nicheformer.ckpt",
    'freeze': False,  # Backbone adaptation strategy
    'extract_layers': [11],  # Feature extraction layers
    'lr': 1e-4,
    'warmup': 1,
    'max_epochs': 50000,
    'batch_size': 12,
    'supervised_task': 'niche_classification',
    'n_classes': 17,
    'organ': 'brain'
}
```

> [!TIP]
> The `organ` parameter determines which data partition to load. For custom datasets, you'll need to add corresponding logic in the configuration system to point to your data paths.

Sources: [_config_embeddings.py](src/nicheformer/config_files/_config_embeddings.py#L1-L6), [_config_fine_tune.py](src/nicheformer/config_files/_config_fine_tune.py#L1-L21)

## Common Usage Patterns

### End-to-End Embedding Extraction Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Load Raw Data] --> B[Apply Basic Filtering]
    B --> C[Align Genes to Model]
    C --> D[Tokenize with Tech Mean]
    D --> E[Load Pre-trained Model]
    E --> F[Extract Embeddings Layer]
    F --> G[Store in AnnData.obs]
    G --> H[Downstream Analysis]
```

### Multi-Task Fine-tuning Setup

When working with multiple downstream tasks, Nicheformer supports layer extraction and reinitialization strategies:

| Strategy | Description | Use Case |
|----------|-------------|----------|
| `freeze=True` | Lock all backbone weights | Small datasets, prevent overfitting |
| `extract_layers=[11]` | Use only last layer | Simple tasks, avoid overfitting |
| `extract_layers=[8,9,10,11]` | Combine multiple layers | Complex tasks, richer features |
| `reinit_layers=[11]` | Reinitialize top layers | Domain adaptation |

Sources: [FineTuningModel](src/nicheformer/models/_fine_tune_model.py#L15-L40), [_fine_tune.py](src/nicheformer/_fine_tune.py#L15-L75)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

### Out-of-Memory Errors

If you encounter CUDA OOM errors during embedding extraction:
- Reduce `batch_size` (try 16 or 8 instead of 32)
- Decrease `max_seq_len` (context window size)
- Use smaller `chunk_size` for data processing
- Enable `precision='bf16-mixed'` for reduced memory footprint

### Slow Data Loading

For large datasets, ensure you're using the distributed data pipeline:
- Verify Merlin DataModule is properly configured
- Increase `num_workers` for parallel loading
- Use `.parquet` files for optimized I/O
- Consider pre-tokenizing data to disk

### Poor Performance on Fine-tuning

If fine-tuning performance is suboptimal:
- Start with `freeze=True` and only unfreeze after initial training
- Use smaller learning rates (1e-5 to 1e-4) for fine-tuning
- Check that your `technology_mean` matches your platform
- Verify gene alignment with the pre-trained model
- Consider increasing `warmup` steps for stable training

Sources: [get_embeddings.ipynb](notebooks/experiments/get_embeddings.ipynb#L1-L100), [MerlinDataModule](src/nicheformer/data/datamodules.py#L118-L132)

# Installation and Setup



This guide walks you through installing Nicheformer, a foundation model for single-cell and spatial omics analysis. We'll cover environment setup, dependency management, and data preparation to get you ready for training, fine-tuning, or extracting embeddings from pre-trained models.

## System Requirements

Before beginning the installation, ensure your system meets the following requirements:

| Requirement | Minimum Version | Recommended Version |
|-------------|-----------------|---------------------|
| Python | 3.9 | 3.9 or 3.10 |
| CUDA (optional) | 12.1 | 12.1+ |
| RAM | 16 GB | 32 GB or higher |
| GPU | 8 GB VRAM | 16 GB+ VRAM for training |
| Disk Space | 10 GB | 50 GB+ for data and models |

Nicheformer requires **Python 3.9 or newer** to function properly. The project is licensed under the BSD 3-Clause License, which allows for both academic and commercial use with proper attribution.
Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L15), [LICENSE](LICENSE#L1-L30)

## Installation Architecture

Understanding the installation architecture helps you navigate dependencies effectively. The following diagram illustrates the relationship between Nicheformer components and their dependencies:

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[Python 3.9+] --> B[Nicheformer Package]
    B --> C[Core Dependencies]
    B --> D[Optional Components]
    
    C --> C1[PyTorch 2.5.1+]
    C --> C2[PyTorch Lightning 2.0+]

    style C2 fill:#ffe1e1
```

![Nicheformer Project Structure](https://github.com/theislab/nicheformer/blob/main/docs/images/project_structure.png?raw=true)

## Quick Installation

The recommended approach uses **Mambaforge** (a lightweight conda distribution) to create an isolated environment, preventing conflicts with existing Python packages. This approach ensures reproducibility and simplifies dependency management.

### Step 1: Create and Activate Conda Environment

First, create a dedicated conda environment with Python 3.9:

```bash
mamba create -n nicheformer_env python=3.9 -y
```

Activate your newly created environment:

```bash
mamba activate nicheformer_env
```

This isolates Nicheformer's dependencies from your system Python and other projects, which is especially important given the specific version requirements for packages like numpy (1.26.4) and pandas (1.5.3).
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L29-L35), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L14-L32)

### Step 2: Clone and Install Nicheformer

Clone the repository and install it in development mode, which allows you to modify the source code if needed:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/theislab/nicheformer.git
cd nicheformer
pip install -e .
```

The `-e` flag enables **editable mode**, linking the installed package directly to the source code directory. This is ideal for development or when you want to track the latest changes from the repository.
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L36-L41), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L10)

> [!TIP]
> **Critical Tip**: Always verify your Python version before installation (`python --version`). Using Python 3.11 or higher may cause compatibility issues with some dependencies, particularly pyensembl and older versions of scientific computing libraries.

## Installation Options

Depending on your use case, you may want to install additional optional dependencies. The following table summarizes available installation options:

| Installation Command | Purpose | Use Case |
|---------------------|---------|----------|
| `pip install -e .` | Core package only | Standard users extracting embeddings |
| `pip install -e ".[dev]"` | Development tools | Contributors modifying source code |
| `pip install -e ".[test]"` | Testing framework | Running test suite |
| `pip install -e ".[doc]"` | Documentation tools | Building documentation locally |
| `pip install -e ".[cuda]"` | CUDA acceleration | GPU-accelerated training |
| `pip install -e ".[dev,test,doc]"` | All extras | Full development environment |

### Developer Installation

For contributors planning to modify the codebase or run tests, install all development dependencies:

```bash
pip install -e ".[dev,test,doc]"
pre-commit install
```

The `pre-commit install` command sets up automated code formatting and linting checks that run before each commit, ensuring code consistency across the project.
Sources: [docs/contributing.md](docs/contributing.md#L14-L20), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L34-L52)

### CUDA Installation

For GPU-accelerated training (recommended for pretraining and large-scale fine-tuning), install CUDA-specific dependencies:

```bash
pip install -e ".[cuda]"
```

This includes NVIDIA cuBLAS, cuDNN, CUDA runtime, and Triton, which are essential for leveraging PyTorch's CUDA capabilities. Note that you must have compatible NVIDIA GPU drivers installed on your system.
Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L54-L59)

python -c "import nicheformer; print(f'Nicheformer version: {nicheformer.__version__}')"

You should see output similar to:

```

import nicheformer

```

## Data Preparation

Nicheformer requires both pre-trained model weights and dataset-specific preprocessing statistics. These must be downloaded and placed in the correct directory structure.

### Download Pre-trained Models

Pre-trained Nicheformer weights are available from [Mendeley Data](https://data.mendeley.com/preview/87gm9hrgm8?a=d95a6dde-e054-4245-a7eb-0522d6ea7dff). Download the model files and place them in the `data/` directory:

```bash
# After downloading from Mendeley Data
# Place files in: nicheformer/data/
ls data/
# Should show: model.h5ad and other model files
```

The pre-trained weights include model parameters from both pretraining and fine-tuning experiments, as well as linear probing results that you can use for downstream analysis.
Sources: [README.md](README.md#L47-L51), [data/README.md](data/README.md#L1-L5)

### Model Means and Technology-Specific Statistics

Technology-specific mean vectors are required for proper data normalization. These are located in `data/model_means/`:

```
data/model_means/
├── cosmx_mean_script.npy
├── dissociated_mean_script.npy
├── iss_mean_script.npy
├── merfish_mean_script.npy
├── model.h5ad
└── xenium_mean_script.npy
```

Each `.npy` file contains mean expression values for a specific spatial omics technology (CosMx, Xenium, MERFISH, ISS, or dissociated single-cell data). These are used during tokenization to normalize gene expression values appropriately.
Sources: [data/README.md](data/README.md#L1-L5), [notebooks/README.md](notebooks/README.md#L1-L5)

### SpatialCorpus-110M Data Scripts

For researchers working with the SpatialCorpus-110M dataset, exemplary loading scripts are provided in `data/spatialcorpus-110M/`:

```
data/spatialcorpus-110M/
├── dissociated/      # Loading scripts for dissociated single-cell data
└── spatial/          # Loading scripts for spatial omics data
```

These scripts demonstrate how to load and preprocess datasets used in the Nicheformer paper. You can customize them for your own data by modifying the appropriate loading functions. The scripts expect data to be organized with `raw/` and `preprocessed/` subdirectories, with the default storing location configurable in `nicheformer.data.constants`.
Sources: [data/spatialcorpus-110M/README.md](data/spatialcorpus-110M/README.md#L1-L9), [src/nicheformer/data/constants.py](src/nicheformer/data/constants.py#L1-L10)

## Troubleshooting Common Installation Issues

| Issue | Symptoms | Solution |
|-------|----------|----------|
| Python version conflict | Installation fails with version requirement errors | Ensure you're using Python 3.9-3.10. Check with `python --version` and recreate environment if needed |
| CUDA incompatibility | GPU training fails with CUDA errors | Verify GPU driver compatibility with CUDA 12.1+. Run `nvidia-smi` to check installed driver version |
| Memory errors during installation | Pip runs out of memory during dependency resolution | Increase virtual memory or use `pip install --no-cache-dir -e .` to skip caching |
| Import errors | `ModuleNotFoundError` when importing nicheformer | Verify installation with `pip show nicheformer` and ensure you're in the correct conda environment |
| PyTorch version mismatch | CUDA not available despite GPU installation | Reinstall PyTorch with correct CUDA version: `pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu121` |

> [!TIP]
> **Critical Tip**: If you encounter version conflicts with dependencies like numpy or pandas, try installing in a fresh environment. The strict version requirements (numpy==1.26.4, pandas==1.5.3) ensure reproducibility but may conflict with other packages in shared environments.

# Downloading Pre-trained Models and Data



This guide explains how to access and download pre-trained Nicheformer models and required data files for your spatial and single-cell omics analysis. Nicheformer provides model weights and auxiliary data through centralized repositories, along with exemplary loading scripts for processing your own datasets.

## Architecture Overview

The data access workflow for Nicheformer follows a modular architecture where pre-trained models, technology-specific parameters, and data loading utilities are integrated. The following diagram illustrates the complete data acquisition and preparation pipeline:

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[Start: Nicheformer Setup] --> B[Download Pre-trained Models]
    A --> C[Download Technology Means]
    A --> D[Prepare Data Structure]
    
    B --> B1[Mendeley Data Repository]
    B1 --> B2[Model Checkpoints<br/>.ckpt files]
    B2 --> B3[data/ Directory]
    
    C --> C1[Technology-Specific Files<br/>.npy files]
    C1 --> C2[data/model_means/ Directory]
    C2 --> C3[model.h5ad Reference]
    
    D --> D1[Create Directory Structure]
    D1 --> D2[raw/ Subdirectory]
    D1 --> D3[preprocessed/ Subdirectory]
    
    B3 --> E[Ready for Fine-tuning]
    C3 --> F[Ready for Tokenization]
    D3 --> G[Ready for Dataset Loading]
    
    E --> H[Use in Embeddings/Fine-tuning]
    F --> H
    G --> H
    
    subgraph "External Repositories"
        B1
    end
    
    subgraph "Local Repository"
        B3
        C2
        D2
        D3
    end
```

## Pre-trained Model Access

Nicheformer pre-training weights are distributed through Mendeley Data, a scientific data repository. These weights represent the foundation model trained on the SpatialCorpus-110M dataset and can be used for transfer learning, embedding extraction, or fine-tuning on downstream tasks. The complete model parameters including pretraining, fine-tuning, and linear probing results are available at [Mendeley Data](https://data.mendeley.com/preview/87gm9hrgm8?a=d95a6dde-e054-4245-a7eb-0522d6ea7dff).

Download the model checkpoint files from Mendeley Data and place them in a convenient location within your project structure. The checkpoint files have a `.ckpt` extension and follow PyTorch Lightning's format. For example usage, you would specify the path like:
```python
checkpoint_path = '/path/to/nicheformer/pretrained_models/your_checkpoint.ckpt'
```
Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L31-L36), [data/README.md](/data/README.md#L1-L5)

## Technology-Specific Mean Files

Nicheformer requires technology-specific mean vectors for normalization during data preprocessing. These mean files are computed across large datasets for each spatial transcriptomics technology and are essential for proper tokenization. The repository includes several technology mean files in the `data/model_means/` directory:

| Technology | Mean File | Description |
|------------|-----------|-------------|
| CosMx | cosmx_mean_script.npy | CosMx spatial transcriptomics platform |
| Dissociated | dissociated_mean_script.npy | Dissociated single-cell RNA-seq data |
| ISS | iss_mean_script.npy | In situ sequencing technology |
| MERFISH | merfish_mean_script.npy | Multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization |
| Xenium | xenium_mean_script.npy | 10x Genomics Xenium platform |

Additionally, the `model.h5ad` file in the same directory serves as a reference AnnData object containing gene information and model specifications used during pretraining. This file is particularly important when loading your own datasets to ensure gene alignment with the pre-trained model. Download or copy these files to your local `data/model_means/` directory to enable proper data processing.

Sources: [data/model_means](/data/model_means), [notebooks/README.md](/notebooks/README.md#L1-L5)

## Dataset Structure Requirements

Before downloading or preparing your datasets, establish the proper directory structure as required by Nicheformer's data loading pipeline. The data organization follows a standardized pattern with `raw` and `preprocessed` subdirectories:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A[Root Data Directory] --> B[raw/]
    A --> C[preprocessed/]
    B --> B1[Dissociated Datasets<br/>.h5ad files]
    B --> B2[Spatial Datasets<br/>.h5ad files]
    C --> C1[Tokenized Datasets<br/>Ready for model input]
    C --> C2[Processed Datasets<br/>With embeddings]
```

The `raw/` subdirectory should contain your original AnnData files (.h5ad format) for both dissociated single-cell data and spatial omics data. The `preprocessed/` subdirectory is where tokenized datasets and data with extracted embeddings are stored. You can configure the default storage location by modifying the `DefaultPaths` class in `src/nicheformer/data/constants.py` to match your local filesystem structure.

Sources: [data/spatialcorpus-110M/README.md](/data/spatialcorpus-110M/README.md#L3-L9), [src/nicheformer/data/constants.py](/src/nicheformer/data/constants.py#L88-L93)

## Downloading GEO Datasets

For datasets available through the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), Nicheformer provides automated download utilities. The `src/nicheformer/data/download.py` module includes functions to download and extract tar archives from GEO with progress tracking. You can download datasets by their GEO accession number using the command-line interface:

```bash
python -m nicheformer.data.download --geo-id GSEXXXXXX --save-path /your/data/raw/directory
```

The download script supports:
- Streaming downloads with progress indicators
- Automatic extraction of tar/zip archives
- Optional file format filtering to extract specific file types only
- Error handling for network issues and corrupted downloads

For programmatic access, you can also use the `download_tar` function directly:
```python
from nicheformer.data.download import download_tar

url = "https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/download/?acc=GSEXXXXXX&format=file"
save_path = "/path/to/your/data/raw/GSEXXXXXX.tar.gz"
download_tar(url, save_path, file_format="h5ad")
```

> [!TIP]
> When using the file_format parameter, you can pass a list to extract multiple formats (e.g., `file_format=['h5ad', 'csv']`) or a single string for one specific format. This is useful when GEO archives contain multiple file types but you only need specific ones.

Sources: [src/nicheformer/data/download.py](/src/nicheformer/data/download.py#L1-L89)

## Exemplary Loading Scripts

The repository provides tokenization notebooks that demonstrate how to process various spatial transcriptomics technologies. These notebooks serve as templates for preparing your own data and are located in the `notebooks/tokenization/` directory:

- `cosmx_human_liver.ipynb` - CosMx human liver dataset
- `cosmx_human_lung.ipynb` - CosMx human lung dataset
- `merfish_mouse_brain.ipynb` - MERFISH mouse brain dataset
- `xenium_human_colon.ipynb` - Xenium human colon dataset
- `xenium_human_lung.ipynb` - Xenium human lung dataset

These notebooks show the complete pipeline from raw data loading through tokenization, including how to apply the technology-specific mean files for normalization. Before using these scripts, ensure you have placed the required model weights and technology mean vectors in the `data/model_means/` directory.

Sources: [notebooks/README.md](/notebooks/README.md#L1-L5), [notebooks/experiments/get_embeddings.ipynb](/notebooks/experiments/get_embeddings.ipynb#L1-L100)

## Complete Setup Example

Here's a complete example showing how to configure paths for embedding extraction using downloaded resources:

```python
import os
from nicheformer.models import Nicheformer
from nicheformer.data import NicheformerDataset

# Configuration with downloaded resources
config = {
    # Path to your preprocessed dataset (in preprocessed/ subdirectory)
    'data_path': '/path/to/data/preprocessed/your_dataset.h5ad',
    
    # Technology mean file from model_means/ directory
    'technology_mean_path': '/path/to/data/model_means/cosmx_mean_script.npy',
    
    # Downloaded model checkpoint from Mendeley Data
    'checkpoint_path': '/path/to/pretrained_models/your_model.ckpt',
    
    # Output configuration
    'output_path': 'data_with_embeddings.h5ad',
    'batch_size': 32,
    'max_seq_len': 1500,
    'aux_tokens': 30,
    'embedding_layer': -1,  # Last layer embeddings
}
```

> [!TIP]
> The model.h5ad file in model_means/ contains the reference gene expression matrix used during pretraining. When loading your own datasets, ensure that your data uses the same gene identifiers or perform appropriate gene alignment to match the pre-trained model's gene space.

## Troubleshooting Guide

| Issue | Possible Cause | Solution |
|-------|---------------|----------|
| File not found errors | Incorrect paths in configuration | Verify paths point to the `data/` subdirectory as specified in README |
| Missing technology mean | Mean file not downloaded | Download the appropriate `.npy` file from the repository or Mendeley Data |
| OOM during loading | Large dataset, insufficient memory | Use the `chunk_size` parameter to process data in batches |
| Gene mismatch | Dataset uses different gene identifiers | Align your genes with `model.h5ad` using gene symbols or Ensembl IDs |
| Download failures | Network issues or corrupted archive | Re-download using the GEO script with error handling enabled |

The complete architecture for data processing, from raw datasets through to model inference, builds upon these foundational resources. Ensure all components are properly configured before proceeding to downstream analysis.

# Understanding Nicheformer Data Schema



This page provides a comprehensive overview of the Nicheformer data schema, which extends the Cellxgene schema to support both single-cell and spatial omics data for foundation model pretraining. The schema is designed to capture rich biological metadata while enabling efficient tokenization and distributed training workflows.

## Core AnnData Schema Structure

Nicheformer builds on the AnnData format with standardized fields for cell-level observations (obs), gene-level variables (var), spatial coordinates (obsm), and unstructured metadata (uns). The schema enforces ontology-based metadata to ensure biological interoperability across datasets.

### Observation Fields (adata.obs)

The observation layer contains cell-level metadata divided into three categories: required ontologies, biological annotations, and Nicheformer-specific fields. All ontology fields must use controlled vocabulary from standard repositories.

**Required Ontology Fields:**

| Field Name | Description | Example Value |
|------------|-------------|---------------|
| `assay_ontology_term_id` | Experimental assay type | `EFO:0030004` (10x 5') |
| `sex_ontology_term_id` | Biological sex | `PATO:0000383` (female) |
| `organism_ontology_term_id` | Species identifier | `NCBITaxon:9606` (human) |
| `tissue_ontology_term_id` | Tissue origin | `UBERON:0002048` (lung) |
| `suspension_type` | Sample suspension type | `cell`, `nucleus`, or `na` (spatial) |

**Biological Annotation Fields:**

| Field Name | Description | Example Value |
|------------|-------------|---------------|
| `cell_type_ontology_term_id` | Cell type classification | `CL:0000066` (epithelial cell) |
| `development_stage_ontology_term_id` | Developmental stage | `HsapDv:0000087` (human adult stage) |
| `disease_ontology_term_id` | Disease state | `MONDO:0002006` (cancer) |
| `self_reported_ethnicity_ontology_term_id` | Ethnicity metadata | `HANCESTRO:0012` (European) |

**Nicheformer-Specific Fields:**

| Field Name | Description | Data Type |
|------------|-------------|-----------|
| `condition_id` | Experimental condition identifier | string |
| `tissue_type` | Tissue origin category | `tissue` or `organoid` |
| `author_cell_type` | Original cell type annotation | string |
| `library_key` | Spatial library identifier | string |
| `niche` | Niche composition identifier | string |
| `region` | Anatomical region | string |
| `dataset` | Source dataset name | string |
| `sample_id` | Sample identifier | string |
| `donor_id` | Donor identifier | string |
| `x`, `y` | Spatial coordinates | float |

Sources: [constants.py](src/nicheformer/data/constants.py#L78-L123), [validate.py](src/nicheformer/data/validate.py#L187-L210)

### Variable Fields (adata.var)

Gene-level metadata supports filtering and cross-dataset alignment:

| Field Name | Description | Data Type |
|------------|-------------|-----------|
| `feature_is_filtered` | Gene filtering flag | boolean |
| `gene_name` | Gene symbol (required) | string |
| `feature_reference` | Genome reference | string |
| `feature_biotype` | Gene biotype | string |

All variables must be indexed by Ensembl Gene IDs (e.g., `ENSG00000139618`) to enable cross-species compatibility.

Sources: [constants.py](src/nicheformer/data/constants.py#L120-L123)

### Multi-dimensional Observation Fields (adata.obsm)

Spatial omics data requires specialized storage structures:

| Field Name | Description | Data Type | Dimensions |
|------------|-------------|-----------|------------|
| `spatial` | Spatial coordinates | float64 array | n_cells × 2 |
| `X_niche` | Niche composition matrix | sparse matrix | n_cells × n_cell_types |
| `X_niche_0` to `X_niche_4` | Multi-radius niche compositions | sparse matrix | n_cells × n_cell_types |

The niche composition matrices capture the cellular neighborhood context by aggregating cell type distributions around each cell within defined radii, enabling the model to learn spatial relationships.

Sources: [constants.py](src/nicheformer/data/constants.py#L113-L117), [niche_compositions.py](src/nicheformer/data/tools/niche_compositions.py#L1-L51)

### Unstructured Metadata (adata.uns)

Global dataset metadata:

| Field Name | Description | Example |
|------------|-------------|---------|
| `title` | Dataset title | descriptive string |
| `niche` | Niche calculation parameters | dict with radius, node_degree |
| `schema_version` | Schema version identifier | string |
| `nicheformer_version` | Nicheformer version | `"0.0.1"` |

Sources: [constants.py](src/nicheformer/data/constants.py#L106-L112), [validate.py](src/nicheformer/data/validate.py#L212-L215)

## Data Processing Pipeline

### Tokenization Strategy

Nicheformer converts normalized gene expression data into fixed-length token sequences through a multi-step process:

1. **Quality Control Filtering**: Remove cells with <200 counts and genes expressed in <5 cells
2. **SCT Normalization**: Scale each cell to 10,000 counts
3. **Technology Scaling**: Divide by technology-specific mean expression
4. **Gene Ranking**: Sort genes by expression (descending)
5. **Token Selection**: Select top expressed genes up to max_seq_len (default: 4096)
6. **Token Offset**: Add auxiliary token offset (default: 30) for padding

```python
# Tokenization process in code
def tokenize_data(x: np.array, median_counts_per_gene: np.array, max_seq_len: int = None):
    x = np.nan_to_num(x)  # Handle missing values
    x = sf_normalize(x)  # Scale to 10,000 counts
    median_counts_per_gene += median_counts_per_gene == 0  # Avoid division by zero
    out = x / median_counts_per_gene.reshape((1, -1))  # Technology normalization
    scores_final = _sub_tokenize_data(out, 4096, 30)  # Gene selection
    return scores_final.astype('i4')
```

The resulting token array has shape (n_cells, max_seq_len) with dtype int32, where each value represents a gene index plus the auxiliary token offset.

Sources: [dataset.py](src/nicheformer/data/dataset.py#L12-L50), [xenium_human_lung.ipynb](notebooks/tokenization/xenium_human_lung.ipynb#L120-L149)

### Spatial Niche Composition

Spatial datasets include neighborhood context through composition matrices. The `niche_compositions()` function computes cellular neighborhoods using radius-based spatial graphs:

```python
def niche_compositions(adata: AnnData, radii: list[float]) -> AnnData:
    # Calculate spatial neighborhoods
    connectivities, _ = spatial_neighbors(
        adata, spatial_key='spatial', library_key='library_key',
        coord_type='generic', radius=radius
    )
    # Aggregate cell type distributions
    one_hot_ct = get_dummies(adata.obs['author_cell_type'], dtype=int, sparse=True)
    niche = connectivities @ csr_matrix(one_hot_ct)
    # Store as obsm
    adata.obsm[f"X_niche_{n}"] = niche
```

This creates sparse matrices where each row represents a cell and columns represent cell types, with values indicating the proportion of that cell type within the defined radius.

Sources: [niche_compositions.py](src/nicheformer/data/tools/niche_compositions.py#L1-L51)

## Distributed Data Format (Parquet)

For distributed training, Nicheformer converts H5AD files to Parquet format optimized for the Merlin data loading framework. The PARQUET_SCHEMA defines 30 columns:

### Expression and Niche Data:
- `X`: int32 array - Tokenized gene expression sequence
- `X_niche_0` to `X_niche_4`: int32 arrays - Niche composition tokens
- `density_0` to `density_4`: float32 arrays - Cell density metrics

### Categorical Metadata (all int64):
- `niche`, `author_cell_type`, `region`, `cell_type`, `development_stage`, `disease`, `tissue`, `tissue_general`
- `assay`, `specie`, `modality`, `organism`, `dataset_id`, `donor_id`, `tech_sample`, `idx`

### Quality Flags:
- `is_primary_data`: boolean - Primary dataset indicator
- `measured_genes`: int32 - Number of genes detected per cell

Sources: [datamodules.py](src/nicheformer/data/datamodules.py#L15-L42)

## Schema Validation

The validation framework extends cellxgene schema compliance with Nicheformer-specific requirements:

### Validation Checks:

1. **Gene Validation**: All genes must be valid Ensembl IDs for the specified organism (mouse or human)
2. **Ontology Validation**: Required ontology fields must use supported vocabulary terms
3. **Nicheformer Validation**: Additional checks for `condition_id` and `tissue_type` presence
4. **Label Appending**: Converts ontology IDs to human-readable labels

```python
def validate(adata: AnnData, organism: Literal["mouse", "human"] = "mouse", 
             ignore_labels: bool = False, verbose: bool = False):
    # Check genes
    gene_checker = GeneChecker(SupportedOrganisms.HOMO_SAPIENS)
    valid_genes = [g for g in adata.var_names if gene_checker.is_valid_id(g)]
    
    # Validate schema
    validator = CurrentFormat(ignore_labels=ignore_labels)
    validator.validate_adata(adata)
    validator.validate_nicheformer(adata)
    
    # Append labels
    writer = AnnDataLabelAppender(validator)
    adata = writer.write_labels()
    
    return adata, validator.is_valid, validator.errors
```

Sources: [validate.py](src/nicheformer/data/validate.py#L24-L70)

## Supported Assay Technologies

Nicheformer supports multiple single-cell and spatial omics platforms through standardized ontology identifiers:

| Technology | Ontology ID | Category |
|------------|-------------|----------|
| 10x Genomics 3' v2 | EFO:0009899 | Dissociated |
| 10x Genomics 3' v3 | EFO:0009922 | Dissociated |
| 10x Genomics 5' v1 | EFO:0011025 | Dissociated |
| 10x Genomics 5' v2 | EFO:0009900 | Dissociated |
| Smart-seq2 | EFO:0008931 | Dissociated |
| MERFISH | EFO:0008992 | Spatial |
| CosMx | EFO:0030029 | Spatial |
| Xenium | (assigned separately) | Spatial |

Each technology requires a technology-specific mean expression vector for proper normalization, calculated across representative datasets.

Sources: [constants.py](src/nicheformer/data/constants.py#L4-L20)

## Dataset Class Implementation

The `NicheformerDataset` class wraps AnnData objects with chunked processing for memory efficiency:

```python
class NicheformerDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, adata, technology_mean, split='train', 
                 max_seq_len=4096, aux_tokens=30, chunk_size=1000,
                 metadata_fields=None):
        # Filter by split
        self.adata = adata[adata.obs.nicheformer_split == split].copy()
        # Process in chunks
        self._process_chunks()
        # Prepare metadata
        self._prepare_metadata()
    
    def _process_chunk(self, start_idx, end_idx):
        # Convert sparse to dense
        x = chunk_adata.X.toarray() if issparse(chunk_adata.X) else chunk_adata.X
        # Normalize and tokenize
        x = sf_normalize(x) / self.technology_mean
        tokens = _sub_tokenize_data(x, self.max_seq_len, self.aux_tokens)
        return tokens
```

This architecture enables loading datasets with millions of cells by processing in configurable chunk sizes with explicit GPU memory management.

Sources: [dataset.py](src/nicheformer/data/dataset.py#L60-L171)

## Complete Data Schema Architecture

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Raw Data Files] --> B[AnnData H5AD]
    B --> C[Required Fields]
    C --> C1[obs: Ontology Metadata]
    C --> C2[var: Gene Information]
    C --> C3[obsm: Spatial/Niche]
    C --> C4[uns: Global Metadata]
    
    B --> D[Quality Control]
    D --> D1[Cell Filtering >200 counts]
    D --> D2[Gene Filtering >5 cells]
    
    B --> E[Tokenization Pipeline]
    E --> E1[SCT Normalization 10k]
    E --> E2[Technology Mean Scaling]
    E --> E3[Gene Expression Ranking]
    E --> E4[Top Gene Selection 4096]
    
    E --> F[Token Array int32]
    F --> G[Parquet Conversion]
    G --> H[Merlin DataLoader]
    H --> I[Model Training]
    
    B --> J[Validation]
    J --> J1[Gene ID Validation]
    J --> J2[Ontology Compliance]
    J --> J3[Nicheformer Extensions]
```

Sources: [dataset.py](src/nicheformer/data/dataset.py#L1-L171), [datamodules.py](src/nicheformer/data/datamodules.py#L1-L186), [validate.py](src/nicheformer/data/validate.py#L1-L259)

## Data Access and Preparation

Preparing data for Nicheformer involves three main stages:

### 1. Data Acquisition
Download datasets from GEO using the download utilities or use provided exemplary loading scripts. Access pre-processed datasets from the SpatialCorpus-110M repository in both dissociated and spatial formats.

### 2. Schema Validation
Run validation to ensure compliance with ontology requirements and Nicheformer-specific fields:
```python
from nicheformer.data import validate
adata, is_valid, errors = validate(adata, organism="human", verbose=True)
```

### 3. Tokenization and Export
Apply the tokenization pipeline with appropriate technology means:
```python
from nicheformer.data import NicheformerDataset
dataset = NicheformerDataset(
    adata, technology_mean=xenium_mean, 
    split='train', max_seq_len=4096
)
```

Sources: [download.py](src/nicheformer/data/download.py#L1-L89), [basic_filtering.py](src/nicheformer/data/tools/basic_filtering.py#L1-L40)

> [!TIP]
> Always use technology-specific mean vectors for normalization to ensure cross-platform comparability. The mean vectors account for systematic biases between different omics platforms and are essential for accurate tokenization across heterogeneous datasets.

> [!TIP]
> For spatial datasets, always include the `library_key` field in spatial neighbor calculations. This prevents incorrect neighbor assignments across tissue sections or experimental batches, ensuring niche composition matrices accurately reflect biological neighborhoods.
